analysis.title: Core Matters: Riding the AI waves through thematic baskets
key_insights: AI has become a broad investment cycle across data centres, semiconductors, software, cloud and power networks, and the opportunity extends beyond frontier model developers to the whole chain from deployment to adoption.

Global AI-related infrastructure investment in 2026 is expected to be about $1 trillion, mostly in the US. Goldman Sachs puts the US part at $581bn. The BIS and Columbia Business School put it at up to $800bn.

Weekly token usage on OpenRouter rose this year from a few trillion to over 150 trillion. Falling AI unit prices have so far been absorbed by faster usage growth, so cheaper AI does not by itself weaken the capex case.

Adoption is broad but shallow. Stanford's AI Index has 88% of surveyed organisations using AI in 2025. A survey of 396 enterprises found only 11% could forecast AI spending within ±10%. Many firms are still in pilot mode.
McKinsey estimates global data-centre capacity demand rising from about 82 GW in 2025 to 219 GW by 2030. AI-related capacity goes from about 44 GW to 156 GW, roughly 70% of the total.

Financing risk is rising. Hyperscaler credit spreads widened from 55bps a year ago to 127bps. Off-balance-sheet commitments at Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Microsoft are $2.4tn, four times the $604bn on their balance sheets (WSJ). The BIS flags AI as a possible source of financial-system fragility.

Competition is commoditising AI. Open-weight models were 56% of tokens through Vercel's AI Gateway in August, up from 7% in December. The report sees the key risk as a redistribution of value across the chain, not weaker demand.

Regulatory risk: a Democratic sweep of Congress in November 2026 could raise scrutiny of data-centre development, permitting, power and water use. The report expects Trump would veto tightening for now.

Power and cooling are becoming the main constraint on AI scaling. Goldman expects data-centre power demand to rise about 220% from 2023 to 2030. A 20-30% US power shortage versus demand is possible through 2028. Morgan Stanley sees data-centre emissions reaching 1.2 Gt by 2030.

Software started recovering in the Q2 earnings season as AI looked less of a threat than feared. Microsoft gave the clearest evidence with stronger backlogs, higher cloud revenue, better free cash flow and better guidance despite higher capex. 2027-28 sales forecasts for hyperscalers and the 23 largest IT stocks rose over the past three months.

US Tech's P/E relative to the S&P 500, on three-year forward EPS, is down 34% from its August 2024 peak to 0.95. Mag 7 trade at a 20% discount to their EPS trend relative to the S&P 493. The derating is not from weaker profitability: 12-month forward ROE is up by a fifth to 43%.

Hyperscaler free cash flow estimates for 2026 and 2027 were cut over three months, while estimates for the 23 largest tech stocks were cut only slightly. The report favours diversification across the AI value chain over a narrow hyperscaler focus.

Positioning is only a partial cushion: investor exposure to Technology is slightly above its historical average, so further outflows are possible if earnings or financing news disappoint. Oracle has derated the most on spending and balance sheet concerns.

The framework has four value-capture layers: Phase 1 Precursors (Mag 7), Phase 2 Infrastructure (94 stocks, with 10 in Phase 2b Cooling), Phase 3 New Revenues (39 stocks) and Phase 4 Enhanced Productivity (94 stocks). Baskets are equally weighted and drawn from US companies above $1bn market cap.

Basket valuations on 12-month forward P/E: aggregate US AI basket 17.9x, 7% below its average since 1995. Infrastructure is +20% versus history, Cooling +39%, New Revenues -46% and Productivity -13%. PEG is 0.5x for Infrastructure, 0.7x for Cooling, 1.1x for Productivity and 1.3x for New Revenues.

Preferred US allocation is Phase 4 Enhanced Productivity, plus selective exposure to Phase 2b Cooling. The Phase 4 preference rests on broad AI diffusion exposure, lower capital intensity and a mid-term earnings path through operational gains that may surprise analyst forecasts, not only on the 13% P/E discount. Phase 3 is seen as deserving its discount given monetisation and execution risk.

China AI basket trades at 18.6x forward P/E versus 25.5x its median since 2015, with a PEG of 0.6x versus 0.9x for US AI. The largest growth-adjusted gap is in cooling, physical AI, monetisation and productivity, with PEG about 0.7 versus 1.1 for US peers. China installed 59% of global industrial robots in 2025.
China-specific risks: export restrictions, less proven monetisation, higher regulatory intervention risk, possible overinvestment from the self-sufficiency push, and weaker governance standards.

The EU AI basket has 79 companies, mostly industrials, IT and financials in the UK, France, Germany and the Netherlands. It trades in line with its own history (17.6x vs 17.5x) with about 15% EPS growth in both 2026 and 2027, and is offered as diversification versus US tech and the EMU index.

sector_views.sector: Productivity beneficiaries (financials, healthcare, consumer discretionary, communication services, industrials)
sector_views.rationale: Broad AI diffusion exposure, lower capital intensity and a possible mid-term earnings gain from operational improvements, at a 13% P/E discount to history.
Structural demand from rising rack density and power use. The basket is +39% versus its history but has a PEG of 0.7x.
Strong capex linkage but valuation is 20% above history, so the report is selective.
The 46% discount to history is seen as reflecting monetisation and execution risk and commoditisation.
Relative P/E is 0.95 versus the S&P 500 and the sector ranks 9th cheapest on the composite valuation ranking. Hyperscaler free cash flow is under pressure.

earnings_insights: Analysts expect the Mag 7 versus S&P 493 EPS growth gap to fall from +19 points in 2026 (31% vs 12%) to zero in 2027 (10% vs 10%), estimate basis, IBES consensus as of 19/10/2026.
Median 2026 EPS growth estimates: US AI baskets 19%, Infrastructure 40%, Cooling 35%, New Revenues 20%, Productivity 14%, MSCI US IT 57%, S&P 500 35% (IBES consensus, as of 19/10/2026).

Q2 2026 reporting season: Microsoft reported stronger backlogs, higher cloud and compute revenue, improved free cash flow and better guidance despite rising capex. Other hyperscalers reported faster cloud revenue growth and data-centre leasing.
Analysts cut 2026-27 free cash flow estimates for hyperscalers over the past three months but only slightly for the 23 largest US tech stocks. 2027-28 sales estimates for both groups rose.

macro_indicators.interpretation: The scale of the build-out. The US share is $581bn per Goldman Sachs and up to $800bn per BIS and Columbia Business School.
Rising debt issuance to fund capex is widening spreads, which pressures valuation multiples.

trade_ideas.description: Overweight a US AI Phase 4 Enhanced Productivity basket (equally weighted, 94 stocks)
trade_ideas.rationale: Broad exposure to AI diffusion, lower capital intensity, a 13% P/E discount and a possible earnings path via operational improvements.

trade_ideas.description: Selective overweight in the US AI Phase 2b Cooling basket (10 stocks)
trade_ideas.rationale: Structural demand from rack density and power use. The +39% premium to history is backed by a PEG of 0.7x.
trade_ideas.risk: Infrastructure capex could run out of steam if hyperscalers struggle to monetise.

trade_ideas.description: Geographic diversification of AI exposure via a China AI basket (infrastructure, physical AI, productivity) and a single EU AI basket (79 stocks)
trade_ideas.rationale: China trades at a PEG of 0.6x versus 0.9x for US AI. The EU basket has about 15% annual EPS growth and trades in line with history.
trade_ideas.risk: China export controls, regulation and governance. EU has few pure-play AI names.

risk_factors: Financing and monetisation: capex is increasingly debt-funded, spreads are widening and returns may disappoint.
Competition and commoditisation: cheaper open-weight and Chinese models compress margins and pricing power.
Regulation: fragmentation across jurisdictions and a possible tightening after the November 2026 midterms or the 2028 elections.
Infrastructure and environment: power, cooling and water shortages, permitting and social acceptance.
Front-loaded earnings from the capex wave may fade as spending slows, and GPU obsolescence may understate depreciation.
Phase 3 software and IT services face disruption from model providers and AI-native challengers.
Tech positioning is slightly above its historical average.
charts_described: Weekly token usage on OpenRouter rises from about 10/24 to over 150 trillion tokens by 07/26, per the report's text.
US Tech P/E relative to the S&P 500 fell 34% from the August 2024 peak to 0.95.
vol_and_positioning: Investor exposure to Technology is slightly above its historical average, leaving the sector exposed to outflows if earnings or financing news disappoint.
Big tech is nearly 40% of the S&P 500, which the report cites as concentration risk.
geopolitical: US midterm elections in November 2026: a Democratic sweep of Congress could increase regulatory scrutiny of AI, data centres, permitting, power and water use.
China export restrictions and geopolitical tensions create uncertainty over China's ability to close the technology gap.
China's push for technological self-sufficiency could lead to excess AI infrastructure capacity.

tension_points.bull_case: Demand supports the capex: token use is above 150 trillion a week, 2027-28 sales forecasts are rising, and Microsoft's Q2 showed stronger backlog, cloud revenue and free cash flow. US Tech has already derated 34% relative to the S&P 500 while ROE rose to 43%.
tension_points.bear_case: Capex is absorbing free cash flow and shifting funding to debt. Spreads have widened from 55bps to 127bps, off-balance-sheet commitments are $2.4tn, and hyperscaler FCF estimates were cut.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Disappointing returns that tighten financing conditions, or earnings or financing news that triggers outflows from Tech given positioning slightly above its average.

tension_points.bull_case: Value should move from scarce-input providers to companies embedding AI into workflows, supporting the Phase 4 productivity basket at a 13% P/E discount.
tension_points.bear_case: Phase 4 gains may not appear as AI revenue, and Phase 2 trades 20% above history on strong demand.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Productivity gains fail to show up in earnings.

theme_stances.key_argument: The next phase of the AI cycle is driven by adoption and productivity gains rather than access to compute.
theme_stances.evidence: our preferred allocation is Phase 4 – Enhanced Productivity

theme_stances.key_argument: Rising rack density and power consumption make thermal management a bottleneck with structural demand.
Rising capex is weighing on free cash flow and shifting funding to debt, widening credit spreads.
